narrative:
The model determined that you have a 63% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward success. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 28, also well below the accepted average of 37, added further concern, though it carried less weight than your school performance. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Stronger grades and a higher test score in a future application would directly address the factors that led to this rejection.
